articles.title: Portuguese police clear Lisbon housing protest camp, arrest 25
articles.summary: Officers baton-charge demonstrators in overnight operation as activists demand government action on housing crisis.
articles.body:
Police in Portugal have cleared a camp in central Lisbon set up to protest against the country’s deepening housing crisis, baton-charging demonstrators and making 25 arrests.

Dozens of officers, some with police dogs, moved in on the camp in Rossio Square shortly after 2am (02:00 GMT) on Sunday.

They had warned protesters that their tents would be dismantled if they were not removed, threatening disobedience charges for those who resisted.

Protesters had pitched more than 100 tents after Saturday’s protest march by thousands along one of Lisbon’s main avenues.

A smaller camp of about 50 tents was also dismantled in Porto’s Praca D Joao I public square, where police made six arrests.

Police said the operation was “proportionate” and that the 25 people arrested in Lisbon were later released and are due in court on Monday.

While police reported seven minor injuries among officers and protesters in the two operations, the activist group Casa para Viver (Homes to Live) said 60 people were hurt and called for a fresh protest outside parliament on Tuesday.

“Choosing the early hours of the morning to unleash dogs and baton-charge peaceful protesters is a political decision. It shows this government would rather repress those denouncing the housing crisis than address it,” the group said.

Portugal is grappling with one of Europe’s most acute home affordability crises, as prices have more than doubled since 2017 while rents for new leases have nearly doubled, with young people among the hardest hit.

Protesters say soaring rents and higher living costs are squeezing households and turning housing into a growing source of discontent.

The Bank of Portugal estimates a shortfall of 300,000 homes nationwide, equivalent to Lisbon’s entire housing stock.

The protesters are demanding that the government scrap a bill to make evictions easier and end rent caps on new leases, which passed a first parliamentary reading, although the far-right Chega party abstained.

The protests in Portugal echo recent demonstrations in Spain over home shortages and surging rents.

There have also been protests in cities including Paris , where small student demonstrations over school conditions broadened into wider protests against government economic policies.

articles.title: Zero-Day Option Traders Are Betting Against Big S&P 500 Swings
articles.summary: While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders...
articles.body:
(Bloomberg) -- While some investors position for AI earnings, geopolitics and interest rates to send stocks either to new highs or into a tailspin, zero-day option traders have increasingly bet that the S&P 500 Index will remain calm.

An analysis of 0DTE options flow from UBS Group AG derivatives strategist Kieran Diamond shows a marked shift toward tactical traders buying calls and selling puts when the market declines, and doing the opposite during rallies. The net effect of what they term a "counter-trend delta bias" is the equivalent of buying low and selling high, which further suppresses swings on the S&P 500.

Zero-day to expiry options have taken on an outsized importance in the daily moves of the equities gauge, with around 66% of the overall volume expiring within a day, according to Garrett DeSimone at OptionMetrics. That's increased the focus on short-term positioning as both retail and institutional traders seek insight on how options flows are influencing the $66 trillion US benchmark index.

"This counter-trend trading pattern seems to be a response to very rangebound markets," said Diamond. "The magnitude of these options flows means that this can start to look self-fulfilling, with options investors helping to limit price moves in either direction."

This intraday tactical shift since 2024 is notable, with larger volumes trading on smaller moves, helping limit S&P 500 realized volatility. The pattern resembles the stabilizing effect of positive gamma, with traders buying into dips and selling into rallies, much like option dealers who are long gamma and similarly buy declines and sell rallies to stay delta-neutral.

The counter-trend trading bias is one factor that has helped contain moves. Another is the long option-dealer gamma regime often seen in the S&P 500, much of which is driven by the prevalence of a big institutional trader selling one-day iron condors — a put spread and a call spread.

RELATED: Popular Zero-Day Trades Curb Stock Rallies: Options Watch

The growth of the 0DTE counter-trend trading flow is now so great that the net effect outweighs the impact from the option dealer re-hedging, according to UBS.

articles.title: How America can bring film and television production home
articles.summary: The newly introduced Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act seeks to implement a federal tax incentive to combat the trend of film and television production moving overseas.
articles.body:
In the classic Western “Shane,” Joey Starrett hears a hard lesson about Rufus Ryker’s ruthless campaign against the homesteaders: “It’s the same old story … and you can’t learn that lesson but once.”

Today, that story is economic and cinematic. And America has learned this lesson more than once: If you take an industry for granted, its jobs, revenue and know-how move overseas and don’t come back.

Film and television production, an export industry with a $9 billion trade surplus , risks following the same script. Forty-five percent of U.S. films and scripted television shows were shot abroad in 2025, up from about one-third three years earlier. That is not just a scene change. It is skilled work, artistry and investment leaving the U.S.

States have responded aggressively. Georgia provides a revealing close-up. It built a robust production hub with incentives of up to 30 percent, attracting billions in spending, building soundstages, and developing a talented workforce. Marvel spent more than $3 billion in Georgia over nearly a decade , including “Black Panther” and two “Avengers” movies. It later shifted much of that work to the United Kingdom, where national incentives changed the math.

Georgia did what it was supposed to do. It built a formidable screen industry. But a state is not a country. States can influence where projects land; they cannot alone ensure those projects stay in the U.S. That is why the newly introduced Motion Picture, Television, and Entertainment Revitalization Act aims to create a federal tax incentive to work alongside state programs.

A federal film incentive should be simple, targeted and accountable. The proposed legislation offers a 20 percent tax credit for U.S. production labor, including crew wages. The credit could rise to 30 percent for independent productions, projects filming in qualifying rural opportunity zones or federally declared disaster areas, or those returning from overseas. The goal is clear: bring more film and television work home and create lasting American jobs.

A single movie or television shoot can employ hundreds and support scores of small businesses. Nationally, the industry supports more than 2 million jobs and $202 billion in wages , and 93 percent of its nearly 162,000 businesses employ fewer than ten people. Most are working- and middle-class jobs. Camera operators and editors, for example, earn a median of around $75,000 a year . Grips, electricians, drivers, costume designers, tailors, set designers, construction workers, casting directors, animators, producers, production assistants, and office staff keep cameras rolling. When production leaves, those paychecks and purchase orders go with it.

This is a national industry. Almost 40 states offer film incentives. Oklahoma reports an economic impact exceeding $531 million from its program. Kentucky notes nearly $795 million in production expenditures since 2022. Pennsylvania projects its 2025-26 credits to generate $1.1 billion in economic activity across 35 counties. Utah’s rural film incentive has driven more than $200 million in spending since 2022.

Still, even strong state programs can be outbid when other countries offer more competitive packages. Sixty-five countries offer national production incentives . Some, like Canada , Australia and Japan , combine them with regional programs, giving them an even greater advantage. A federal incentive won’t diminish competition among states; it will strengthen their ability to compete globally while rewarding those that innovate most.

Any federal incentive must include commercials. They are a vital economic pillar of the industry. When commercials leave, a dependable source of work and benefits goes with them. Thousands of middle-class professionals depend on them for income as well as health insurance and pension coverage.

Commercial production has hollowed out at home as shoots move overseas , where countries aggressively court and often win the business. That same dynamic can work in America’s favor, allowing communities across the country to compete for that work.

Many states, including Texas , Pennsylvania , Arizona , Ohio , and Nevada , include commercials in their incentive programs because they create well-paying jobs. A federal credit can enhance that approach, making it easier to produce domestically without forcing people to compete globally by accepting lower rates. The bill currently excludes commercials . That needs to change.

The fair question is whether a federal incentive is a sound investment for the taxpayer. To pass that test, the credit should remain tied to verified U.S. employment, with clear accountability measures so taxpayers can see the results.

The industry won’t stand still. Global competition, changing audience habits, and new technologies are rewriting the script. Disruption isn’t necessarily a threat; it can be an opportunity if America strengthens the infrastructure that generations have built and prepares for the next act.

New filmmakers and storytelling formats will emerge from established studios, independent creators, and platforms not yet invented. The question is whether workers, artists and businesses can build that future here.

The next great American story can come from anywhere. Let’s make sure it gets made in America.

James Babbin is a film and audio producer, an actor and a member of the Coalition for American Production .

Georgia House members on Thursday Feb. 29, 2024 voted to limit transfers of Georgia’s lucrative film tax credit and require moviemakers do more to get the top tax credit rate. articles.title: When will there be a flying car in your garage? Not anytime soon.
articles.summary: People have been wishing for flying cars since the earliest days of flight and automobiles. Does Tesla’s demonstration earlier this month of a “flying” version of its new Roadster mean we’re close?
articles.body: People have been wishing for flying cars since the earliest days of flight and automobiles. Does Tesla’s demonstration earlier this month of a “flying” version of its new Roadster mean we’re close? If you’re looking for a car that can safely travel on roads and highways while also flying significant distances, then no. But if you want a personal flying machine that operates at relatively low altitudes and travels the distance of most car trips, that’s closer to reality. Enter the fast-growing world of electric vertical take-off and landing aircraft, known by the somewhat cumbersome acronym of eVTOLs. They can’t travel on highways, and some don’t even have wheels. But many companies have been racing to develop vehicles straight out of science fiction movies and cartoons, with a few already selling aircraft. “The idea of the ‘flying car’ has captured the public imagination for generations, and today that excitement is driving real investment and innovation across the industry,” said Kristina Menton, vice president of flight at Pivotal, one of the companies making eVTOLs. “The appeal is easy to understand. Why spend 90 minutes in traffic when you could spend 20 minutes in the sky?” The eVTOLs are very lightweight compared to traditional cars, with limited carrying capacity, and can generally fly 100 miles at a time at most. They also can’t operate on roads. But even without driving over asphalt, some proponents believe eVTOLs should be considered an automobile in the strictest definition of that word – a vehicle that can transport you from point A to point B. Flying “cars” can appeal to drivers who want to avoid “roads (that are) are problematic and congested,” said Rani Plaut, cofounder and CEO of Air, an Israeli company that plans to build eVTOLs at a facility in Florida. One company that claims to be developing a true flying car is California start-up Alef. CEO Jim Dukhovny said the initial version, which will have a top speed of about 55 mph, was designed to be both an aircraft and a car instead of adapting one or the other. The 254-pound vehicle uses eight propellers inside its body to get airborne but also has four wheels and is designed for driving. The “Model A” can only carry one person that weighs less than the empty vehicle and doesn’t have standard safety equipment like airbags. But Dukhovny wants it to be thought of as a car, not an eVTOL. “EVTOLS are for the aviation market,” he said, “Our competition is Toyota, Ford, Tesla.” But trying to do both, operate as a car and an aircraft, faces many basic engineering problems, said Roger Connor, curator of the vertical flight collection at the Smithsonian’s National Air and Space Museum. That’s because aircraft are sensitive to weight, while cars need heavy equipment. “Something that is a hybrid between the two is going to be a poor-performing aircraft and a poor-performing vehicle,” he told CNN. Still, the Federal Aviation Administration has pushed for the development of eVTOLs, launching a series of testing programs across 26 states in March. “The future of aviation is here — and it’s going to dramatically improve how people and products move,” said Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy when announcing the program. One thing the FAA is investigating is who will be allowed to fly these aircraft. The expectation is that it will take far less training to fly an eVTOL than to pilot a small plane, helicopter or passenger plane – perhaps as short as a few days. But that is still a work in progress, Connor said. “We haven’t licensed anybody in these new category aircraft yet,” he told CNN. “This is little bit of a new thing for everybody, and it is especially so for the FAA, since the aircraft are not airplanes and they’re not helicopters.” Despite an appetite from the FAA, eVTOLs are still very much in development. Very few have been built and delivered to customers, and those available are very expensive. Larger versions, or “air taxis” that carry a handful of passengers, will cost more than $1 million each, Connor said. Those for personal use will retail for less, but still cost anywhere from $60,000 up to $400,000 for a two-seat aircraft with some endurance and range. “For $60,000, you’re basically getting a fancy drone that could carry 160 pounds or so for maybe 10 minutes,” he added. Tesla has yet to say how much a “flying” version of its Roadster will cost, and no version, flying or grounded, will be for sale until at least 2028. Unlike most eVTOLs, which use propellers, the Roadster utilized compressed air jets to leap over other cars and propel from the top of a ramp six or seven stories high during its product reveal earlier this month. The Roadster also did not fly any appreciable distance, landing short of even the 120 feet the Wright Brothers achieved during their first flight at Kitty Hawk, North Carolina, in 1903. Tesla’s own site cautions the test model is “not approved for public road use.” Still, the splashy demonstration has many in the industry cheering. “When a company with Tesla’s reach puts the idea of everyday people leaving the ground in front of millions of viewers, it widens the conversation, and the industry benefits from that curiosity,” said Pivotal’s Menton. But she cautions that her company is not a car company. “We build aircraft, not flying cars,” she said.
